scoring: an answer scores 1 if its verdict matches; full credit also requires naming the missing hypothesis for REJECT items

items.claim: For almost every initial row, the centre column has frequency 1/2.
items.reference: RequestProject/GLM/Rule30/Ergodic.lean (Problems 1 and 2 hold for almost every row)

items.claim: Hence the centre column of the single-cell seed has frequency 1/2.
items.missing_hypothesis: the seed is a measure-zero row; 'almost every' says nothing about it
items.next_test: a seed-specific argument using the seed's initial data

items.claim: The map x -> a(n)(0) has ANF degree 2n-1 for 2 <= n <= 20.
Therefore the single bit a(n)(0) is hard to compute.
items.missing_hypothesis: degree is a property of the map on all rows, not of its value on the seed
items.next_test: a uniform machine model with a lower bound (Problem3 in MachineModel.lean)

items.claim: The seed value a(n)(0) equals the linear ANF coefficient, so the parity of whiteDiagonalCount (the top coefficient) tracks the seed.
items.missing_hypothesis: the linear and the top coefficient are different coefficients; the first equals the seed value by definition, the second is a map property
items.next_test: state a seed-specific recurrence for the linear coefficient and test it

items.claim: The first 10^6 centre bits have wobble |D(n)| <= 2*sqrt(n) except at listed times.
So the infinite centre column has frequency 1/2.
items.missing_hypothesis: finite-prefix data alone cannot decide an asymptotic property; a finite certificate needs a structural theorem behind it
items.reference: RequestProject/GLM/Rule30/WobbleCertificate.lean: no finite certificate decides Problems 1 or 2
items.next_test: a structural argument (e.g. a proof that the total echo is o(N^2))

items.claim: A sequence that passes a 24-bit block-uniformity test on 10^6 bits is normal; one that fails is not.
items.missing_hypothesis: normality is asymptotic; the binary Champernowne sequence (normal) fails this test at 10^6 bits
items.next_test: state the asymptotic property and look for a proof

items.claim: Problem 2 asks whether the centre column is a normal sequence.
items.missing_hypothesis: Problem 2 asks only for frequency 1/2 of each colour (balance); normality needs every k-block with frequency 2^-k

items.claim: Every right diagonal of the seed pattern is periodic, with period dividing 2^D and least period > ceil(D/2).
So the diagonal read-out a(t) = rdiag(t, t) is aperiodic.
items.missing_hypothesis: unbounded diagonal periods hold for every right-white row, including rows with periodic centre columns
items.next_test: use the seed's initial diagonal data (only diagonal 0 black at time 0)

items.claim: The seed's right edge is white, so the first inner diagonal is driven only by the left edge.
items.missing_hypothesis: the right edge a(t)(t) is always black, and the right-diagonal system is autonomous (diagonal D depends only on D-1, D-2)

items.claim: The centre column is the output of a fixed nonlinear shift register driven by the periodic edge stripes, so its pseudo-randomness follows from filter-generator theory.
items.missing_hypothesis: a finite-state machine driven by an eventually periodic input has an eventually periodic output; the model needs an unbounded register (the diagonal read-out)
items.next_test: work with the unbounded diagonal system and the seed's initial data

items.claim: D(N)^2 = N + 2 * (sum of the lag-k echoes of the +-1 wave, 1 <= k < N).
Showing the wave has no spectral atom (no resonance) is an easier route to Problem 2 that bypasses the combinatorics.
items.missing_hypothesis: 'no atom at frequency 0' in the Cesaro sense is equivalent to Problem 2, so it is a restatement, not a shortcut
items.next_test: a seed-specific bound on the total echo

items.claim: If the centre column were eventually periodic with period p, its normalised lag-p echo would tend to 1.
No causal predictor beats chance on a typical (random) row.
So no predictor beats chance on the seed's centre column.
items.missing_hypothesis: the centre column is computable; the Rule 30 rule itself predicts it perfectly. Unpredictability is only meaningful relative to a declared rule space
items.next_test: fix a rule space (lag, finite-state) and prove escape or typicality for it

items.claim: Problem 1 is equivalent to the centre column escaping all lag rules 'bit t repeats bit t-p', and also to escaping all finite-state rules.
Rule 30 with a right-white initial row always produces an aperiodic centre column, because the dynamics is chaotic.
items.missing_hypothesis: some right-white rows have centre column 1,0,1,0,... (captured by a lag-2 rule)

items.claim: whiteDiagonalCount(n) equals the number of zeros of a Boolean function of n-1 variables.
whiteDiagonalCount(n) is odd for n <= 36, so the top-monomial conjecture is proved.
items.missing_hypothesis: exhaustive checks cover finitely many n (Lean proves 2 <= n <= 20; n <= 36 is outside-Lean evidence)
items.next_test: a recurrence or involution for the reduced function valid for all n

items.claim: Lifting a tied Leech-lattice address into a Lorentzian space resolves the tie and therefore adds evidence about Rule 30.
items.missing_hypothesis: a symmetry-preserving lift introduces no new evidence and can preserve the tie
items.next_test: compare the lattice encoding against a direct encoding on a retrieval task
